summary: Describes an EDNS(0) option for DNS Update requesters and authoritative servers to include a lease duration in an update or its response. The server can then clean up stale records that were added by updates but never renewed.

eli5.summary: If you leave a note on a shared board, it should disappear after a while unless you renew it. This lets DNS records have an expiry date so old ones get tidied away.

subtitle: A DNS Update extension that gives records an expiry date, so abandoned ones get cleaned up.

tldr.problem: Records added with DNS Update are often never deleted, for example when a laptop leaves Wi-Fi range, so stale data can stay on the authoritative server indefinitely.
tldr.mechanism: An EDNS(0) Update Lease option carries a lease duration in the update and the granted duration in the response. Requesters must refresh before the lease runs out, or the server stops publishing the records.
tldr.outcome: Servers can garbage collect records that were not renewed, and the option is the lease mechanism that RFC 9665 relies on for service registration. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Refresh time
facts.value: 80% of the lease plus a 0% to 5% random offset

facts.label: Recommended server limits
facts.value: Max 24 hours (LEASE) and 7 days (KEY-LEASE); min 30 seconds

today: RFC 9664 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and RFC 9665 uses it for the lifetimes of service registrations.

sections.title: Why DNS Updates Need Leases
sections.content:
DNS Update (RFC 2136) lets a host change its own entries in the Domain Name System, so a persistent hostname can follow an IP address that changes over time. That is especially handy for mobile hosts.

The catch is that mobile hosts often vanish without cleaning up. The RFC's example is a user who publishes address records and then moves their laptop out of range of the Wi-Fi access point: the records with stale information may stay on the authoritative DNS server indefinitely. The fix is an extension that tells the server to delete records automatically after a period of time unless they are refreshed.
sections.eli5: If you write your address on a school noticeboard and then move away, your old address stays up forever. A lease makes the note expire so the board does not fill up with outdated information.

sections.title: The Update Lease Option
sections.content:
The lease travels in an Update Lease option inside the EDNS(0) OPT pseudo-record (RFC 6891) of a standard DNS Update message. Every such message MUST include the OPT record, and that record MUST include the option. The option code is UPDATE-LEASE (2).

The LEASE field is an unsigned 32-bit integer in network byte order, giving a duration in seconds. In a request it is the duration the requester wants. In a response it is the duration the server actually granted, which may be less than, greater than, or equal to the request.

There are two variants. The 4-byte variant has only LEASE, and it applies to every record in the Update section. The 8-byte variant adds KEY-LEASE: LEASE applies to everything except KEY records, and KEY-LEASE applies to KEY records. KEY records get their own lease because RFC 9665 uses them to reserve a name while the service itself is absent. Records that are removed are permanently removed.
sections.eli5: The note carries a number saying how long the pin should stay up, counted in seconds. A second, optional number says how long to keep a special name tag reserved.

sections.title: Requesting and Granting Leases
sections.content:
A requester MUST send an Update Lease option with any update to records that are not meant to stay forever. It SHOULD ask for no less than 1800 seconds (30 minutes), though it MAY ask for less if the records will change more often, and should ask for longer if they are fairly static. A Registration Request adds information that is not thought to be on the server already.

A server that supports the option MUST include one in the response to any successful update (RCODE 0) that carried one. It MAY change the numbers: longer leases to cut refresh traffic, or shorter ones to shorten the life of stale data. The requester MUST use the durations the server returned, whether shorter or longer. If the response has no option at all, the server does not support it, and the requester SHOULD keep sending refreshes as if the server had returned the same option it sent.

Because older, pre-standard peers may only know the 4-byte variant, a server that gets the 8-byte variant MUST answer with the 8-byte variant. A server that gets the 4-byte variant MUST treat it as both the lease and the KEY lease and MUST answer with the 4-byte variant, so the key and the other records expire together. A requester that sent the 8-byte variant and gets the 4-byte one back does the same.

For the first Registration Request after startup, the requester MUST wait a random delay between 0 and 3000 milliseconds, with granularity of no more than 10 milliseconds. This stops many devices of the same type from hitting the server together after a power failure.
sections.eli5: You ask the board keeper to keep your note up for a certain time. The keeper may say yes, or offer longer or shorter, and you have to go by whatever the keeper says. After a power cut, everyone waits a random moment before asking so there is no stampede.

sections.title: Refreshing a Registration
sections.content:
A Refresh Request is an update that renews the lease on an earlier registration without changing anything. It uses the same format as other lease updates, and it MUST carry an Update Lease option. It should not include prerequisites that would fail whether or not the earlier records are still there, so that if the server lost them, for example in a reboot, the refresh simply adds them again. An update that changes the server state from a previous registration is a Registration Request, not a Refresh Request.

When a lease update succeeds, the requester computes a deadline of 80% of the lease duration plus a random offset of 0% to 5% of it, and MUST send a Refresh Request when that time arrives if the data should stay advertised. The random offset keeps refreshes from synchronizing. If no response comes, the requester should retry sensibly; with 15% to 20% of the lease left this need not be aggressive, and the RFC suggests nine more retries spaced evenly until the expiration time.

A requester with several registrations on one server MAY coalesce them into a single Refresh Request, putting all its records on the same schedule. It does so once at least one record has used up 75% of its lease, and over UDP it MUST NOT coalesce if that would truncate the message. Requesters SHOULD NOT refresh when every record still has more than 50% of its lease left, although early refreshes are allowed, for example for a sleepy device whose radio is already on.

On a valid Refresh Request the server MUST send an acknowledgment containing the new lease, and MUST NOT bump the zone serial number if the zone contents did not change. If the refresh does change the zone, the serial number MUST be updated.
sections.eli5: You should walk back to the board before your note falls off, not at the last second, and everyone picks a slightly different time so they do not all arrive together. If one trip fails, you try again a few times.

sections.title: Garbage Collection
sections.content:
When a record's lease runs out without a refresh, the authoritative server MUST NOT return that record in answers to queries. It MAY delete the record from its database. The lease durations returned to the requester are the ones used to decide when a lease has expired.

For every record except a KEY record, the lease is the LEASE value. For KEY records it is KEY-LEASE if that was included, and otherwise the LEASE value applies to all records in the request.
sections.eli5: Once a note's time is up, the keeper stops showing it to visitors, and may throw it in the bin.

sections.title: Limits and Security
sections.content:
A lease that is too long is not much different from none, so servers should have a default upper bound on both LEASE and KEY-LEASE. Defaults of 24 hours and 7 days respectively are RECOMMENDED. A lease that is too short raises server load and risks records vanishing early, so servers MUST have a default minimum; 30 seconds for both values is RECOMMENDED, although in most cases much longer leases, for example an hour, SHOULD be used. Operators MAY be allowed to change both limits.

A malicious or buggy requester could renew at a high rate to overload the server, a risk the RFC says also exists for ordinary updates, so servers should follow established best practices against flooding over UDP and TCP. Some authentication should be used for updates: a shared secret (RFC 8945) or public key signing such as SIG(0) (RFC 2931), with keys of limited authority so that one compromised key does not expose whole zones. Key management is out of scope. The RFC also notes that RFC 9665 pairs these leases with First Come, First Served naming rather than an explicit trust process.
sections.eli5: The keeper needs rules: notes cannot stay up forever, and cannot be so short-lived that people spend all day re-pinning them. The keeper should also check who is pinning and stop anyone who keeps pestering.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA updated the DNS EDNS0 Option Codes (OPT) registry for value 2, with the name Update Lease, status Standard and reference RFC 9664.
sections.eli5: The official list of DNS option numbers now says that number 2 means Update Lease.
